transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-01
Start time (UTC): 16:00
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Hannah Voss (Redwood CSM), Aisha Rahman (Ventana CTO), Tom Beckett (Ventana Lead ML Eng), Ravi Patel (Ventana DevOps), Sofia Miles (Clinical SME)
Recording ID: ff-20260501-ventana-001

Summary:
Quick discovery focused on model selection for clinical note summarization and triage workflows, evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private options. Main concerns: long context (6k-12k tokens), multilingual (EN + ES + PT), tool-calling for EMR fetch & de-identification, compliance (SOC2/audit logs/KMS), and latency vs cost tradeoffs for near-real-time triage. Redwood AE/SE to share benchmark harness and pricing.

Topics covered:
- Workload and throughput expectations
- Context length distributions and long-document handling
- Multilingual requirements and quality thresholds
- Tool-calling patterns (EMR connectors, document retrieval, PII scrubber)
- Security/compliance: KMS, SSO, SOC2, audit logs
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment tradeoffs

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for hopping on, um, want to do quick intros and then dive into the three things you sent over in the email yesterday — Aisha, do you want to kick us off?
[00:12] Aisha: Yeah hi thanks, so Ventana builds clinical decision triage for outpatient clinics, basically we ingest notes, voice transcriptions, and external labs, then the LLM produces a short triage summary and suggested next steps. Our main ask is something that can handle long clinical context — like 6k typical, peaks to 12k tokens when you include notes + lab history — and we need tool calling to fetch patient data and run a PII scrubber before writing results.
[00:34] Tom: And to add, accuracy in Spanish and Portuguese is important, especially for patient-facing summaries, so we'll need multilingual evals. Performance wise we want sub-800ms tail for the majority of triage calls but can tolerate a couple-second tail for heavy contexts.
[00:48] Luis: okay thanks, that's helpful. Quick clarifying question — when you say tool-calling, is that synchronous call-out to your EMR, or batch retrieval ahead of time?
[00:55] Ravi: it's a hybrid — we prefer a synchronous call pattern where the model can request the EMR id and then we return structured results; for very large histories we also pre-fetch and attach as context.
[01:05] Maya: got it. So there's two patterns, pre-fetched context vs on-demand tool call. Either is supported, just different latency/cost tradeoffs.
[01:12] Sofia: one more clinical note — we need deterministic redaction for PHI before anything leaves our network, so ideally key management stays with us for the scrubber keys.
[01:21] Maya: good point. We'll talk about KMS and private deployments shortly. Luis, do you want to walk through the model options that map to this?
[01:26] Luis: sure. So, at a high level there are three deployment patterns that Redwood customers commonly choose: hosted API for fastest time-to-market, Dedicated reserved capacity if you need predictable throughput and lower per-token costs, and Private (VPC / on-prem) for strict data residency and key control.
[01:40] Luis: For the model family choices, since you mentioned long context and multilingual, the candidates are larger open models with extended context support and commercial LLMs. For example, some open LMs support 32k contexts after fine-tune/quantization but at higher latency; other medium-sized models with optimized KV cache give better tail latencies but cap at 8k.
[01:56] Tom: can you be concrete — like which named models?
[01:59] Luis: sure, examples — LlamaX-32k style forks, Mosaic v7-32k variants, some of the Mistral extended context branches, and then there are commercial options like OpenAI's 32k context sibling or Anthropic's Claude-extended. Each has different token costs and latency profiles. I should note the transcript of model names may get fuzzy here — sorry if I mangle some vendor names.
[02:19] Aisha: how about quantization — our infra team is worried about hallucinations with extreme quantization that might affect clinical accuracy.
[02:26] Luis: totally valid. We typically recommend 8-bit quantization for production inference as a good balance; 4-bit can be a cost win but you need to validate on clinical prompts — Redwood Optimize gives quantization recommendations and we'll run evals against your safety/eval set.
[02:37] Ravi: on the dedicated vs hosted question — is key management possible in hosted? We want customer KMS if possible.
[02:43] Maya: hosted offers envelope encryption; we can integrate with your KMS for dedicated and private definitely, hosted can integrate via a customer-managed key with some constraints — we'll send the exact KMS compatibility matrix.
[02:55] Tom: you mentioned KV cache — can you explain how that helps long context?
[02:59] Luis: yeah, KV cache means we avoid re-encoding the full prefix each inference step; for repeated documents we can cache chunk embeddings or kv states so token processing is cheaper. For very long docs we also recommend retrieval-augmented patterns: chunk the history, retrieve top-k chunks, and stream to the model. That keeps your effective context smaller and reduces cost while preserving recall.
[03:18] Sofia: but in clinical timeline use cases we sometimes need entire history for context — is retrieval safe enough?
[03:23] Luis: in many cases yes, especially if you tune retrieval and add a reranker; for edge cases where absolute full-history is required we can use a model variant that supports 32k and combine with caching. There's a cost/latency hit.
[03:34] Aisha: what's the expected difference in latency between hosted and dedicated for a 8k token request?
[03:39] Luis: rough ballpark — hosted using our shared clusters with an optimized model might see median latency 350–600ms for generation up to 2k tokens; for 8k token context generation it's highly workload-dependent but expect 1–3s median; Dedicated on equivalent GPUs with private pools generally reduces tail latency by ~20–40% and predictable capacity avoids queuing spikes. Those numbers depend on batching and continuous batching settings.
[03:58] Ravi: batch settings — if we want sub-second tails, we probably need to avoid batching, right?
[04:03] Luis: yes, there's a latency vs throughput tradeoff — continuous batching helps throughput but increases tail; Redwood Optimize can recommend per-route configs to keep your triage route low-latency and other background jobs batched.
[04:13] Tom: about multilingual — do you do fine-tuning per language or rely on base multilingual models?
[04:17] Luis: both are common. Many open models have decent multilingual capability out of the box; for clinical-grade quality we often run a small supervised fine-tune on your labeled Spanish/Portuguese test set and couple that with prompt engineering and evals. That reduces mis-summarization.
[04:29] Aisha: who typically owns deployment complexity — our infra team or Redwood? We want minimal ops lift.
[04:34] Maya: Hosted is fully managed so minimal ops on your side, Dedicated has more setup (we provision reserved pools but Redwood handles runtime), Private/on-prem requires more customer ops since keys and networking are local, but we provide deployment tooling and runbooks. If you want minimal ops & can accept shared infra, hosted is easiest.
[04:49] Ravi: for Private, do you support air-gapped installs?
[04:52] Luis: yes, our Private package includes on-prem manifests for air-gapped environments; you still get the control plane locally or an offline control plane depending on the option. We'll send the on-prem checklist.
[05:01] Sofia: can Redwood run the PHI scrubber before the model sees it?
[05:04] Luis: yes that's a standard pattern — you can run an in-house scrubber and only send de-identified payloads, or we can run your scrubber in a private network in a Dedicated VPC before handing off to the model.
[05:13] Aisha: how are audit logs surfaced? We require per-request logs for compliance.
[05:17] Maya: we provide audit logs with redaction, plus per-request tracing and token-level cost breakdowns in the Console. For Private, logs can stream to your SIEM directly.
[05:27] Tom: any gotchas for function/tool calling? Example: model wants to call the EMR API to fetch allergy list — what's the recommended design?
[05:33] Luis: typical flow: model outputs a structured function call, Redwood routes the call to your adapter (webhook) which can call EMR and return structured JSON. You control auth and don't have to expose credentials to the model. For high-security setups, run the adapter inside your VPC and use VPC peering.
[05:47] Ravi: are there retries or idempotency guards for tool calls? We need to avoid duplicate writes to the EMR.
[05:52] Luis: yes, we support idempotency keys and you can enforce idempotent adapters; Redwood can also record the function call in the audit trail so you can reconcile.
[05:59] Aisha: pricing question — for a pilot of 200k tokens/day, what's the rough monthly cost hosted vs dedicated?
[06:05] Maya: rough estimate without exact model chosen: hosted might be $2k–5k/month depending on model variant; Dedicated starts with a fixed reservation (eg 1–2 GPU nodes) so unit cost drops if you commit. Luis will run a specific estimate with your context/avg generation length.
[06:17] Tom: and is there a discount if we bring our own license for a model?
[06:20] Luis: yes if you BYO-model images for Private deployment we can price differently; for hosted we have approved model catalog and licensing constraints. We'll document the options.
[06:29] Hannah: quick note on pilot scope: suggest we run two small pilot routes — 1) short context triage (<=2k tokens) on hosted to validate flow, 2) longer context (8–12k) on Dedicated/Private to measure latency and quality — that gives you apples-to-apples comparisons.
[06:45] Aisha: that sounds good to me. We'll need Redwood to provide the test harness so our ML team can run synthetic loads.
[06:51] Luis: yes we'll share a benchmark harness (curl + sample prompts + scoring script).
[06:56] Maya: any security red flags from your side we should know about?
[06:59] Ravi: main ones — KMS integration, firewall egress rules, and the ability to prevent model outputs from being cached outside our control.
[07:06] Luis: we can support customer-managed KMS, we document egress IP ranges, and caching policies can be configured per-route; for example you can disable any persistent cache for routes with PHI.
[07:16] Tom: do you support SAML/SCIM provisioning for RBAC?
[07:20] Maya: yes SAML SSO, SCIM for provisioning, role-based access controls in the Console. We'll share the SSO/SCIM setup doc.
[07:27] Sofia: one small point — our clinicians often paste in dictated notes with timestamps and audio chunks; is audio-to-text part of this or do we feed transcripts?
[07:34] Aisha: we plan to feed post-processed transcripts, we don't need Redwood to run STT for the pilot.
[07:39] Luis: okay that simplifies things a bit.
[07:40] [pause / background keyboard clacking; 00:08 silence]
[07:49] Maya: real quick, a question on evaluation metrics — what are your pass/fail thresholds for the Spanish summaries?
[07:54] Sofia: clinically we need >= 95% recall on medications and allergies, and acceptable fluency measured by clinician review; we'll share a small labeled dataset for scoring.
[08:03] Tom: and we have about 50 annotated examples per language to start.
[08:07] Maya: perfect — that will make fine-tune/eval straightforward.
[08:11] Luis: next, for the data path, if you want zero egress we recommend Private on-prem with customer KMS. If you can accept outbound to a region in the EU or US, a Dedicated VPC is often a sweet spot. Hosted is simplest but requires contractual controls and dedicated key options.
[08:29] Aisha: any limitations on model size for Private installs?
[08:33] Luis: mainly hardware — we support common GPU types in our on-prem package; if you want a 70B or 100B model you'll need multi-GPU nodes and NVLink setups; we can help size it.
[08:43] Ravi: on that, we run on-prem GPUs already. What's the support model for hardware failure?
[08:48] Luis: Redwood offers a support add-on that includes hardware runbooks and emergency assistance; for Private we often arrange a joint runbook and a few hours of SRE support during pilot.
[08:58] Aisha: timeline — we want to decide on pilot scope within two weeks and start a pilot mid-May. Is that realistic?
[09:03] Maya: yes, realistic. We'll action the benchmark & pricing share this week.
[09:07] Tom: are there any existing customers in the healthcare space you can point to?
[09:10] Maya: yes we have a couple of health-tech references — we'll share contact details in the follow-up, mindful of NDAs.
[09:16] Ravi: last thing — can the Console surface per-route token usage broken down by model and by user?
[09:21] Hannah: yes per-route, per-token cost breakdown, latency heatmaps, and user-level activity for auditing.
[09:28] Aisha: sounds good. Let's recap next steps.
[09:31] Maya: recap: Redwood shares benchmark harness, SE runs cost/latency estimate for 2 configs (hosted optimized model vs Dedicated 1–2 GPU pool) and Dedicated pricing; customer shares PII/redaction requirements and small labeled eval sets; schedule pilot kickoff week of May 11.
[09:46] Aisha: agreed. Thanks everyone.
[09:48] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up in email.
[09:51] [meeting ends]

Notes on transcription quality: occasional vendor/model name garbling (Mosaic, Mistral, LlamaX variants), minor speaker overlaps.
